title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
goal: Check that a rule gives a definite result and finishes.

prerequisites.text: You can multiply, divide with a remainder and distinguish starting data from a result. The first topic’s program frame is retained.

sections.title: From the task to an operation
paragraphs: Express 125 seconds as whole minutes and remaining seconds. A minute has 60 seconds: two groups fit into 125 and 5 seconds remain. An algorithm is a precise sequence of steps for cases like these.

In C++, / between integers gives the integer quotient and % gives the remainder. The divisor is always 60 here, so division by zero cannot occur. Check the result: 2 × 60 + 5 = 125 and 0 ≤ 5 < 60. This is a postcondition, a property after execution.

Our steps execute once, so they finish. A repeating algorithm needs a separate reason to finish: for example, one fewer item remains after each step. A useful property kept by the steps is called an invariant: the processed part has already been counted correctly. Check a concrete calculation before proving a general case.

sections.title: Check that a rule gives a definite result and finishes.
trace: Set a nonnegative number of seconds.
The remainder is below 60; 2 × 60 + 5 reconstructs the input.

sections.title: Change one condition and check the prediction
paragraphs: Exactly one minute leaves no remaining seconds.
For zero, both quotient and remainder are zero.

sections.title: When the result differs
paragraphs: Printing only minutes loses 5 seconds: the algorithm finished but did not provide the complete required result.

sections.title: Now solve your own task
paragraphs: Split 190 seconds into minutes and seconds. Check reconstruction of the input and the remainder bounds.
Practice contains a separate starter. Predict the result before changing your program. Returning to the example does not replace your source.

selfcheck.prompt: What output follows the specified change? Set seconds to 60, then to 0.
selfcheck.feedback: Exactly one minute leaves no remaining seconds. For zero, both quotient and remainder are zero.

selfcheck.prompt: Split 190 seconds into minutes and seconds. Check reconstruction of the input and the remainder bounds.
selfcheck.feedback: Compare the output with the readable reference case below. Explain each change using the objects or operations in this topic. For 190 seconds, both values are needed: 3 minutes and 10 seconds; 3 × 60 + 10 = 190 and the remainder is in 0..59. Printing only minutes loses 10 seconds.

terms.definition: The intended action of each step is unambiguous.
